newsitem.title: USA: Judge throws out some rape charges against sergeant.
newsitem.headline: Judge throws out some rape charges against sergeant.

text.p: A military judge Thursday dealt a setback to prosecutors of an Army sergeant charged with raping 10 women trainees by throwing out 19 federal sex-crime charges against the soldier, who still faces military charges.

Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston granted a defence pre- trial request and, based on federal law, threw out 16 counts of sexual intercourse by fear and three counts of sodomy by fear against Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, Simpson's attorneys and an Army spokesman said.

Simpson, a drill instructor at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground, is still charged with rape and sodomy under military law for the same incidents. In all he faces 129 counts of sexual misconduct and other crimes.
But prosecutors now must meet a higher definition of forcible sex to win a conviction, said Simpson's civilian defence attorney, Frank Spinner.
"It will make it harder for the government to prove a rape charge," Spinner told reporters after Johnston informed attorneys of his decision outside of court.

That is because the military's rape laws require a fear of death or great bodily harm to justify a lack of resistance by the victim, as opposed to federal standards that require a lesser level of fear.

Simpson would be the first of 10 soldiers charged in a major sexual misconduct scandal at the proving ground to go to trial. The trial is scheduled to start April 14, preceded by jury selection next week.

Johnston's ruling apparently accepted defence arguments that the military rape law took precedence over the federal Sexual Abuse Act of 1986. Military code allows prosecutors to charge soldiers governed by military law with federal crimes unless Congress indicates military law takes precedence.
Prosecutors had argued that Congress envisioned the forcible sex by fear crimes as distinct from rape, and that Simpson should face both the military and federal charges.
Spinner said the defence is confident of winning on military rape and sodomy charges, but that it could also have defeated the federal-based charges.
In a closed court hearing Thursday, Simpson's lawyers sought approval to introduce at his upcoming trial evidence related to past behaviour of his alleged victims.

The request indicated his lawyers might argue that any relationships Simpson had were consensual, echoing media reports that the Aberdeen Proving Ground where he was based had a climate of pervasive sexual activity.

"I think that by the time all the witnesses have testified, both government and defence, I think that everyone will have a fairly accurate picture of what's been going on at Aberdeen Proving Ground," Spinner said.

An article in the Washington Post Sunday, based on interviews and court records, described the Aberdeen base as having a climate of unusually pervasive sexual activity among trainees and between trainees and their superiors.
Asked if he would argue that Simpson only engaged in consensual sex, Spinner said, "we'll discuss what pleas will be entered at another time."
"Our position is that Sgt. Simpson did not rape anyone," he said earlier.

But Spinner said it would be hard to paint in court a "broad brush" argument based on the base's sexual climate, because military court rules require that any evidence of a witness's sexual behaviour must be relevant to the specific issues of the case.
